title: Does Buy Now Pay Later Affect Your Credit Score?
description: Does buy now, pay later affect your credit score? What Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm, PayPal and Zip check and report, and the risk of stacking plans.
keywords: does buy now pay later affect credit score klarna credit score afterpay affirm credit reporting bnpl
takeaways: Most Pay in 4 plans use a soft check and are not reported, but Affirm reports all plans to Experian.
Missed payments can bring late fees and collections, whichever app you use.
The real risk is stacking several plans. Track them all in one list.
body:
Split a purchase into four small payments, pay no interest, and never think about your credit score. That is the promise of buy now pay later. For a long time, it was mostly true. The apps did not report your payments, and lenders could not see what you owed. That changed in 2025. One of the biggest providers now reports every plan to two of the three major credit bureaus, and FICO has built credit scores that read buy now pay later data directly. So the honest answer is: it depends on the app you use, the plan you pick, and whether you pay on time. This guide goes provider by provider. ## The short answer For a standard Pay in 4 plan, applying will not hurt your score. Almost every big provider uses a soft credit check, which other lenders cannot see and which has no effect on your score. What happens after that depends on the provider: - Affirm reports all of its plans, including Pay in 4, to Experian and TransUnion. On-time payments go on your record, and so do late ones. - Klarna, Afterpay, PayPal Pay in 4 and Zip do not report standard Pay in 4 plans. Paying on time builds nothing, because nobody outside the app sees it. - Every provider on this list can hurt you if a balance goes unpaid long enough to reach a collection agency. Collections do get reported, and they are bad news on any credit file. ## The three ways BNPL can touch your credit ### 1. The credit check when you apply There are two kinds of credit check. A soft check is a quick look at your credit file. It shows up only to you, and it cannot lower your score. A hard check is a formal inquiry, the kind you get with a credit card application. Hard checks are visible to other lenders and can knock a few points off your score for a while. Standard Pay in 4 plans from Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm, PayPal and Zip all use soft checks. You can be approved or turned down and your score will not move. Hard checks turn up on some longer monthly financing plans. If one is involved, the provider has to tell you before you agree. ### 2. Whether your payments get reported This is where providers split into two camps. If your provider reports your plan, it appears on your credit report as a small installment loan. Pay on time and it becomes a positive record. Pay late and that is on the record too. Affirm works this way now. Since April 1, 2025, Affirm has reported all payment activity, including on-time, late and missed payments, to Experian. Plans that started on or after May 1, 2025 are also reported to TransUnion. Late payments stay in the reported history even after you catch up. If your provider does not report, your good behaviour earns you nothing on your credit file, and a single late payment usually stays between you and the app. Klarna's Pay in 4, Afterpay, PayPal Pay in 4 and Zip sit in this camp for their standard plans in the US. One catch: reporting and scoring are not the same thing. Affirm's data now sits on your Experian and TransUnion reports, but many scores lenders use today still do not count these small loans. In June 2025, FICO launched BNPL versions of its Score 10 that do count them, and lenders choose which score to use. So your Affirm history is on your file today, and it counts for more each year. ### 3. What happens if you stop paying This is the route that catches people out. A provider that never reports your on-time payments can still hand an unpaid balance to a debt collector, and the collector reports to the credit bureaus. A collection is a serious negative mark that can sit on your file for years. Before that, most providers charge a late fee and pause your account until you catch up. Affirm is the exception on fees: it charges no late fees at all. Its risk is different. Your late payment goes straight onto your credit report instead. ## Provider by provider: checks, reporting and late payments Here is the US picture for standard Pay in 4 plans. | Provider | Credit check | Reports Pay in 4 payments? | If you pay late | |-----------------|---------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Klarna | Soft check | No. Monthly financing plans are reported to Experian and TransUnion | Late fee of up to $7. Unpaid balances can be sent to collections | | Afterpay | Soft check | No | Late fee, capped at 25% of the order value. Account is paused. Unpaid debt can go to collections | | Affirm | Soft check to check eligibility | Yes. All plans reported to Experian since April 2025, and to TransUnion for plans from May 2025 | No late fees. Late and missed payments are reported and stay in the history | | PayPal Pay in 4 | Soft check | No. Pay Monthly loans can be reported | No late fees. Serious delinquency can be reported or sent to collections | | Zip | Soft check | No | Late fee of up to $7. Unpaid debt can go to collections | Two things in that table cause most of the confusion. Klarna's Pay in 4 stays off your credit report in the US, but its monthly financing is a real installment loan, and that one is reported. Same app, two very different credit footprints. And Affirm is the only big provider that treats Pay in 4 like ordinary credit. If you want on-time payments to count for something, Affirm records them. The trade-off is that a bad month gets recorded too. Zip also charges a small installment fee on its plans, so a Zip plan is not quite the free split it looks like at checkout. Check the fee on your own plan before you agree. ## The risk nobody states plainly: stacking Here is the part the checkout screen never shows you. Each app can only see its own loans. Klarna cannot see your Afterpay plan. PayPal cannot see your Zip plan. And because most of these loans never reach your credit report, lenders cannot see the full stack either. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau studied this market using data from six large providers. In 2022, about 63 percent of BNPL borrowers had more than one loan running at once at some point in the year, and about a third used more than one provider. Stacking is not unusual behaviour. It is the normal pattern. Here is an illustration with made-up numbers. Say you split four ordinary purchases in one month: - Headphones, $200 on a Pay in 4 plan: $50 due every two weeks - Shoes, $120: $30 every two weeks - A jacket, $160: $40 every two weeks - Groceries and household bits, $80: $20 every two weeks Each one felt small at checkout. But in the two weeks when all four plans overlap, $140 leaves your account, on top of rent, bills and everything else. Miss one payment because the money was not there and you add a late fee, or a mark on your credit report if the plan is with Affirm. None of the four apps did anything wrong, either. Each one checked you for its own small loan and said yes. The total was never checked by anyone except you. ## If you are outside the US The table above is the US picture. The rules differ elsewhere, sometimes a lot. **United Kingdom.** Klarna is a regulated lender in the UK, and it says it is legally required to report Pay in 3 and Pay in 30 payment data to TransUnion, Experian and Equifax. Late and unpaid balances are visible on your credit file to other lenders. The same company that keeps Pay in 4 off your US credit report reports its UK plans as a matter of law. Do not assume the US rules travel with you. **Canada.** The pattern looks closer to the US. Afterpay's Canadian site says it does not run credit checks to assess creditworthiness and does not report late payments to credit bureaus, pausing accounts instead. The collections risk still applies. **Australia.** Australia changed its laws on June 10, 2025. Buy now pay later contracts now sit inside the national credit framework, providers must hold an Australian credit licence, and credit checks are part of opening an account. Applications and missed payments can show on your credit report there in a way they often do not in the US. ## How to use BNPL without hurting your credit Used one plan at a time, with payments you have already budgeted for, BNPL is a reasonable way to spread a cost. The trouble starts with the stack. These habits keep you on the right side of it: - **Keep a list of every open plan.** App, amount, and the date each payment comes out. The apps will not do this across providers, so it has to be you. A simple spreadsheet does the job, and we have a free one ready if you do not want to build your own.

Download the free BNPL Payment Tracker (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The buy now, pay later tracker listing four plans with each payment, payments left, amount still owed and next payment date](/assets/img/posts/bnpl-payment-tracker-preview-1280x639.webp) - **One or two open plans at a time, at most.** If a third checkout starts calling, stop and check the list first. - **Line payments up with payday.** A payment that leaves the day after payday rarely bounces. One that leaves the day before often does. - **Pay from a debit card or bank account, not a credit card.** Paying a BNPL plan with a credit card just moves the debt, and card interest can start on top. - **If a payment is going to fail, act before the due date.** Most providers let you move a payment date or talk to a hardship team. That conversation is easier before the payment bounces than after. If you are trying to build a credit history rather than just spread a cost, BNPL is mostly the wrong tool, since most plans are never reported. A small credit card paid in full each month does that job properly. See [how to build credit from scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/) for a step-by-step route. If BNPL has already turned into a pile of card debt as well, [how to pay off credit card debt fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/) walks through a payoff plan that starts with the most expensive balance. The urge to split every checkout is worth a look too: [how to stop impulse spending](/blog/how-to-stop-impulse-spending/) covers the habits that stop most stacks before they start. And a quick scan of your open plans fits neatly into [the 20-minute monthly money review](/blog/monthly-money-review/), so nothing rolls into a second month unnoticed. ## Frequently asked questions ### Does buy now pay later build credit? Usually, no. Most Pay in 4 plans are never reported to the credit bureaus, so on-time payments do not raise your score. The main exception in the US is Affirm, which reports all plans to Experian and TransUnion. Even then, the score a lender uses has to be one that counts BNPL data, and many still do not. ### Can buy now pay later hurt my credit score? Yes, in three ways. A hard credit check on a longer financing plan can cost a few points. A reported plan paid late, such as an Affirm plan, puts a late mark on your report. And any unpaid balance that reaches a collection agency can be reported by the collector, whichever app it started with. ### Does Klarna affect your credit score? In the US, Klarna's Pay in 4 uses a soft check and is not reported, so normal use does not change your score. Its monthly financing is reported to Experian and TransUnion, so that product can help or hurt. In the UK, Klarna reports its Pay in 3 and Pay in 30 plans, and late payments show on your file. ### What happens if I miss one BNPL payment? It depends on the provider. Most charge a late fee and pause your account until you catch up. Affirm charges no late fee but reports the late payment. One missed payment on an unreported plan will not usually touch your score. Leaving a balance unpaid until it reaches collections will. ### Is buy now pay later better than a credit card? A Pay in 4 plan paid on time costs nothing and stays off your credit file, but it builds no credit history and offers weaker purchase protection than a card. A credit card charges heavy interest if you carry a balance, but it reports every month and can build your score. Neither one fixes a stretched budget. *Disclaimer: This article is general information about how buy now pay later reporting works, not financial advice for your situation. Provider policies change often, and several changed during 2025. Check your own plan's terms in the app before you rely on any detail here. If you are struggling with repayments, a free debt advice service can help.* ## Sources - [Affirm Help Center, "Understanding credit reporting"](https://helpcenter.affirm.com/s/article/understanding-your-credit) - [Klarna, "Does Klarna perform a credit check and will this affect my credit score?"
